content: The Nurses' Health Study, initiated in 1976 by Dr. Frank Speizer, and the Nurses' Health Study II, launched in 1989 by Dr. Walter Willett, are among the most comprehensive and long-term epidemiological studies focusing on the health of older women. These studies have tracked 121,700 female registered nurses since the mid-1970s to investigate risk factors for cancer and cardiovascular disease. They represent some of the largest research efforts ever undertaken to examine risk factors for chronic diseases in women. The studies involve a multidisciplinary team of clinicians, epidemiologists, and statisticians based at the Channing Laboratory. Collaborating institutions include Harvard Medical School, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. In 1980, the study expanded to include assessments of dietary habits, aspirin use, and colon examinations. The original cohort consisted of nurses aged 30 to 55 years, who were surveyed biennially starting in 1976. Over time, additional questions were incorporated to enhance the scope of the research. Mortality follow-up, which relies on reports from next of kin or postal authorities, has achieved a remarkable success rate of over 98%. In cases of suspected cardiovascular disease or coronary heart disease, follow-up investigations extended beyond death certificates to include autopsy reports and other medical records, where available and permissible. The studies have resulted in the publication of over 100 peer-reviewed papers, covering a wide range of topics. For example, one study evaluated the risks and benefits of low-dose aspirin and vitamin E in preventing cardiovascular disease and cancer in women, involving 39,876 female health professionals aged 45 years or older. Another significant investigation, conducted over eight years, examined the relationship between a low-fat diet and health outcomes in nearly 49,000 postmenopausal women. The research has yielded critical insights into various health topics, including the impact of smoking, dietary patterns, hormone use, and physical activity on chronic disease risk. For instance, studies have explored the relationship between cigarette smoking and myocardial infarction, the use of postmenopausal hormones and coronary heart disease, and the effects of dietary fat and trans fatty acids on cardiovascular health. Other investigations have examined the role of moderate alcohol consumption, whole-grain intake, and physical activity in reducing the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. The findings have also addressed the influence of body weight, weight changes, and obesity on cardiovascular outcomes, as well as the effects of dietary components such as folate, vitamin B6, and omega-3 fatty acids on heart disease and stroke risk. Additionally, the studies have explored the association between sleep duration, snoring, and the development of diabetes and hypertension. Overall, the Nurses' Health Study has provided a wealth of evidence that has shaped public health recommendations and clinical guidelines, particularly in the areas of diet, lifestyle, and chronic disease prevention. Its contributions to understanding the interplay between various risk factors and health outcomes in women remain unparalleled in the field of epidemiology.
